subsection: 1. Nutritional significance and structure of meat

notes.b: Meat is not one food but three groups, and each differs in colour, fat and the nutrients it is valued for.
points: Red meat is beef, lamb, pork and veal, the flesh of mammals, and it is the group most people mean by "meat".
Poultry is chicken, turkey and duck. The breast is paler than the leg or red meat because it contains less myoglobin (the red pigment that stores oxygen in muscle).
Poultry fat is lower than in most red meat, and most of it sits in and under the skin, so poultry is not fat free.
Offal is the edible organs of the animal, such as liver, kidney and heart.
Liver is the richest source of vitamin A, iron and several B vitamins among the offal, which is why offal is valued as cheap, nutrient-dense food.
notes.tip: Do not describe offal in detail beyond liver, kidney and heart, and do not call poultry fat free: say most of its fat is in and under the skin.

notes.h: Nutritive value: protein, fat and carbohydrate in meat
notes.b: Nutritive value is about the nutrients meat contains. Meat is valued mainly for its protein, haem iron and B group vitamins, while its fat is mostly saturated and it supplies essentially no carbohydrate.
points: Protein: meat is a high biological value (HBV) protein, meaning it supplies all the essential amino acids (those the body cannot make) in the proportions the body needs.
Meat is about 20 to 30 per cent protein by weight.
Protein supplies amino acids for growth and repair of body cells and for making enzymes, hormones and antibodies.
Fat: meat fat is mainly saturated, and meat is about 10 to 30 per cent fat, varying with the animal, the cut and whether visible fat is trimmed. Chicken is lower in fat.
Fat gives concentrated energy and insulation, and offal carries fat-soluble vitamins.
Carbohydrate: meat contains essentially none, so it is served with a starchy food such as potatoes, pasta, rice or bread to supply energy and balance the meal.
notes.tip: For each nutrient, name the nutrient, name its source in meat and give its function. Always mention that meat has essentially no carbohydrate and say what to serve with it.

notes.h: Nutritive value: minerals, vitamins and water in meat
notes.b: Besides its macronutrients, meat is an important source of iron and B vitamins, but it is deficient in vitamin C. Water and flavour compounds make up the rest of its character.
points: Haem iron (the form of iron found in animal foods) is present in red meat, offal and the dark meat of poultry. The body absorbs it more readily than non-haem iron from plant foods.
Iron is used to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood, and myoglobin, which stores oxygen in muscle.
Zinc supports enzyme activity, potassium supports muscle function, and phosphorus supports bones, teeth and energy release. Sulphur is present in the sulphur-containing amino acids.
Sodium is high only in processed meat.
B group vitamins help the body release energy from food. Cobalamin (B12) occurs naturally only in animal foods.
Vitamins A and D are found mainly in liver. Meat is deficient in vitamin C (it is not a source), so serve it with vegetables or fruit.
Water makes up about 50 to 60 per cent of meat. Raw lean meat is about 70 to 75 per cent water, so the figure varies with fat content and cooking.
Extractives are flavour compounds that dissolve out during cooking. They give meat its savoury taste and stimulate digestive juices.
notes.tip: Name haem iron for the blood, B vitamins, and A and D in liver. Remember meat lacks vitamin C, and do not forget that the muscle pigment is myoglobin, not haemoglobin.

notes.b: Dietetic value is about how suitable meat is for different people. Some groups gain a great deal from it, while others need to limit it.
points: Growing children and teenagers need meat protein for growth, and adults need it for repair and maintenance of tissue.
Haem iron is especially important for pregnant women, menstruating women (including teenage girls), children and teenagers, to prevent iron-deficiency anaemia.
Older people and anyone with a poor appetite do well on tender, lean or minced cuts cooked gently, because tough or overcooked meat is harder to chew and digest.

People with raised cholesterol or coronary heart disease, and anyone controlling weight, should limit saturated fat and cholesterol. They choose lean cuts, trim visible fat, remove poultry skin, grill rather than fry and limit processed meats.
Low-income households find cheaper cuts and mince good value protein and iron.
Vegetarians and vegans do not eat meat, so they need other sources of protein of similar quality, iron and B12.

Department of Health healthy eating guidelines and the Irish Food Pyramid place meat in one shelf with poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts. They recommend lean and unprocessed choices and advise limiting red and processed meat because of their salt and saturated fat content.
notes.tip: Keep dietetic points separate from nutritive ones. Say which groups need meat (children, teenage girls, pregnant women, those recovering) and which limit it (heart disease, high cholesterol, weight control), with lean cuts and trimming.

notes.b: Meat is muscle, and its structure explains how it feels to eat and why some cuts are tougher than others. Muscle is built from fibres, connective tissue and fat.
points: Muscle is made of long, thin fibres, each a single muscle cell, lying parallel and running in the direction of the muscle's pull.
Groups of fibres form bundles, and the bundles are held together by connective tissue.

Each fibre contains myofibrils made of the proteins actin and myosin, the contractile proteins, which slide past each other to shorten the muscle. The fibre is surrounded by muscle fluid containing water, extractives, soluble protein, vitamins and minerals.
Connective tissue wraps fibres and bundles and attaches muscle to bone through tendons. It contains collagen (white and tough) and elastin (yellow and stretchy).
Fat is found as marbling between and within the muscle fibres, as a layer under the skin or as a covering layer, and around the organs. Marbling adds juiciness and flavour, and fat melts on cooking.
A tougher cut has longer, thicker fibres and more connective tissue.

Diagram: draw a cross-section of muscle showing a bundle of fibres inside a sheath of connective tissue, with one fibre enlarged to show myofibrils (actin and myosin) and a label for fat (marbling). Label connective tissue, fibre, bundle and fat.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe muscle fibres, connective tissue and fat, and to draw a labelled sketch of a muscle fibre bundle.

notes.b: Meat contains several different proteins. Some do the work of the muscle, some carry colour and some form connective tissue, and cooking affects each differently.
points: Myosin and actin are the contractile proteins of the myofibrils and make up most of the fibre protein. They coagulate (set solid) and firm up on heating.
Globulin is a soluble protein in the muscle fluid. It coagulates on heating and is partly lost in drip and cooking juices.
Myoglobin is the red oxygen-storing pigment of muscle and gives raw meat its colour. It denatures (changes shape) on heating, so the meat changes from red to brown or grey.
Collagen is an insoluble connective tissue protein that is tough when raw. It converts to soluble gelatine in slow moist cooking.
Elastin is a springy connective tissue protein in tendons and ligaments. It is very tough and cooking does not soften it, so it is removed or the meat is minced.
notes.tip: Be able to name two meat proteins and give one effect of cooking on each. Collagen and elastin are both connective tissue but only collagen softens, so do not say both do. Meat colour comes from myoglobin, not haemoglobin.

keyTerms.definition: The edible organs of an animal, such as liver, kidney and heart.
A protein that contains all the essential amino acids in the proportions the body needs.
Iron found in animal foods, absorbed by the body more readily than the non-haem iron in plant foods.
A thread-like structure within a muscle fibre, made of actin and myosin, that contracts to shorten the muscle.
A thick contractile protein in myofibrils that works with actin to shorten the muscle.
A thin contractile protein in myofibrils that slides along myosin during muscle contraction.
A tough, insoluble connective tissue protein that converts to gelatine when cooked slowly in moisture.
A springy connective tissue protein found in tendons and ligaments that is not softened by cooking.
The red, oxygen-storing pigment in muscle that gives raw meat its colour.
Fat deposits lying within the muscle, which give meat juiciness and flavour.

factCards.term: Two proteins that make up myofibrils
Three types of fat found in meat
factCards.definition: Marbling within the muscle, a layer of fat under the skin, and fat around the organs.

factCards.term: Four functions of protein in the body
factCards.definition: Growth, repair of body cells, making enzymes and hormones, and making antibodies for immunity.

factCards.term: Three nutrients meat supplies in valuable amounts
factCards.definition: Haem iron, cobalamin (vitamin B12) and high biological value protein.

factCards.term: Two vitamins found mainly in liver

factCards.definition: Collagen, which becomes gelatine when cooked slowly in moisture, and elastin, which cooking does not soften.

questions.prompt: Name two proteins found in meat and state two functions of protein in the body.
questions.model: Any two proteins named, one mark each: myosin, actin, globulin, collagen, elastin or myoglobin. Two functions, one mark each: growth; repair of body cells; making enzymes; making hormones; making antibodies. Credit a function linked to the named protein, such as myosin and actin enabling muscle contraction for movement.

questions.prompt: Give an account of the nutritional significance of meat in the diet, referring to protein, fat, carbohydrate, minerals and vitamins.
questions.model: Protein: HBV protein supplying all essential amino acids; about 20 to 30 per cent of meat; needed for growth, repair, enzymes and hormones. Fat: mainly saturated; energy and insulation; amount varies with animal, cut and cooking method; limit for coronary heart disease. Carbohydrate: none, so serve with potatoes, pasta or bread. Minerals: haem iron in red meat, poultry and offal for haemoglobin and preventing anaemia; zinc for enzyme activity; potassium for muscle function; phosphorus for bones and energy release. Vitamins: B group vitamins for releasing energy from food; B12 found only in animal foods; vitamins A and D in liver; no vitamin C. Dietetic note: needs for growing children, pregnant women and teenagers; processed meats high in salt and saturated fat.
